With the launch of the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro variant, Apple has quietly killed one of the machine's most appealing features. While the two new Mac minis look nearly identical to the previous generation on the outside, Apple has shut off the hidden feature that made the last Mac mini such a great value.

When the M4 Mac mini launched, it was an absolute bargain. Not only did it pack Apple's M4 SoC, it also came with 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. With student pricing of just $599 or $499, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple's lineup, it was also the best value in the entire range.

Video: Apple Killed the Mac mini's Best Hidden Feature :(

However, Apple's smallest Mac always had a secret weapon that made it even more of a bargain: a slot for storage upgrades. Users could actually pry open the back of the machine, unscrew a few screws, and access a removable NAND module, easily swapping in a third-party SSD with capacities up to 2TB.

The benefits were many. Not only could you upgrade the SSD or make it easier to repair a failed drive, you could also save a significant amount of money—skipping Apple's custom upgrade options and handling it yourself with a much cheaper third-party SSD.

Back then, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade at $800, instantly turning this "affordable" computer into a $1,400 machine. If you bought it and then upgraded with a third-party SSD yourself, users could save nearly $500.

Of course, as someone who loves to tinker, I was extremely excited about this and even made a full video tutorial walking through every step of upgrading the stock SSD with a third-party drive. The video did pretty well, racking up 500,000 views.

Video: How to Upgrade the SSD on the M4 Mac mini

Good times don't last forever.

With this new generation of Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly to the logic board, completely eliminating the possibility of any aftermarket NAND module upgrades.

The Mac mini has gone from being arguably the best-value Mac by a mile to a noticeably more expensive product—not only has the base model jumped from $600 to $900, but the 2TB upgrade option has also gone from $800 to $1,000.

Today, if you want an M6 Mac mini with 2TB of SSD, you'll have to pay Apple $1,900. By comparison, an equivalent M4 Mac mini, if upgraded to 2TB with an aftermarket drive, cost around $920 back then, including the roughly $320 aftermarket upgrade cost. Of course, prices have gone up across the board, so this comparison isn't entirely fair to Apple (you can see where I'm going with this), but the difference is a full $1,000, and it's not just because Apple raised prices—it's because Apple removed users' ability to upgrade themselves.

I can roughly guess why Apple raised the base Mac mini by $300, and I can understand why their SSDs cost so much more. Parts, SSDs, and memory have all gotten more expensive because of AI and other factors. But that doesn't explain why Apple didn't keep the removable SSD like before and instead soldered it to the logic board.

We can speculate, but we may never know the real reason why Apple went back to a soldered SSD approach. What we do know is that these machines are noticeably more expensive, and that's honestly putting it mildly. Comparing an M4 Mac mini with a 2TB aftermarket upgrade to an M6 Mac mini with a 2TB custom upgrade, it's roughly 106% more expensive.

9to5Mac's take

While it may not be easy to find a reasonably priced base-model M4 Mac mini on the used market, if you do find one, it's still an outstanding computer for its base performance, features, and upgradable SSD.

The only silver lining is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, so adding fast external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs is a breeze. I'm personally a big fan of the Samsung T9, which is a relatively affordable storage expansion option.

What do you think is the reason Apple killed the Mac mini's removable SSD? Any particular theories? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
